title: Multimodal Models
summary: Multimodal models understand more than one type of data at once, such as images and text together. CLIP aligns images and text in a shared space, and vision-language models can describe images or answer questions about them. Whisper transcribes speec
content:
# Multimodal Models ##### 40,000 photographs and no labels A crafts marketplace in Jaipur had a problem that money could not easily solve. Their catalogue held 40,000 product photographs uploaded by artisans across Rajasthan — block-printed textiles, blue pottery, lac bangles, mojari footwear. The images were beautiful. The metadata was a disaster: sellers typed "beautiful item" or "handmade" or nothing at all. Search did not work, because there was nothing to search. The classical fix would be a labelled dataset and a trained classifier. But their categories were not fixed — sellers invented new product types constantly, and any fixed label set would be stale in a month. They used CLIP instead. No training, no labelled data: ```python categories = ["block printed cotton fabric", "blue pottery vase", "lac bangles", "mojari juti footwear", "miniature painting", "brass utensil", "bandhani dupatta"] # Embed images and text labels into the SAME space, then compare ``` 92% agreement with human categorisation. Two days of work, zero labelling cost. And when a seller started listing a new craft, they added one line of text. **That is what a shared embedding space buys you.** Text and images become comparable, and suddenly you can search images with words, classify with no training examples, and build systems that reason across modalities. ##### What multimodal means So far every model in this course has handled one type of data. A multimodal model processes two or more together — most commonly images and text, increasingly audio and video too. The central technical challenge: an image is a grid of pixels, text is a sequence of tokens. They have nothing in common. **You need to project both into a shared representation space** where distance means something across modalities. Three broad families: | Family | Does | Examples | |---|---|---| | **Aligned embeddings** | Puts images and text in one vector space | CLIP, SigLIP | | **Vision-language models** | Understands images, generates text about them | GPT-4V, LLaVA, Claude, Gemini | | **Speech models** | Audio to text and back | Whisper, TTS models | ##### CLIP and contrastive learning CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) is the foundation, and its training idea is beautifully simple. Take 400 million (image, caption) pairs scraped from the web. Two encoders — a vision transformer for images, a text transformer for captions. For each batch of N pairs, compute all N×N similarities. **Train so that matching pairs have high similarity and every mismatched pair has low similarity.** ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph BATCH["A batch of N image-text pairs"] I1["🖼 blue pottery vase"] --> IE["Image encoder
ViT"] I2["🖼 lac bangles"] --> IE I3["🖼 mojari shoes"] --> IE T1["'a blue pottery vase'"] --> TE["Text encoder
Transformer"] T2["'colourful lac bangles'"] --> TE T3["'embroidered mojari'"] --> TE end IE --> S["N × N similarity matrix"] TE --> S S --> L["Maximise the diagonal
Minimise everything else"] L --> R["Shared embedding space
images and text comparable"] ``` The loss is symmetric cross-entropy over both rows and columns of that matrix: ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def clip_loss(image_embeds, text_embeds, temperature=0.07): """Symmetric contrastive loss.""" image_embeds = F.normalize(image_embeds, dim=-1) text_embeds = F.normalize(text_embeds, dim=-1) logits = (image_embeds @ text_embeds.T) / temperature # (N, N) labels = torch.arange(len(logits), device=logits.device) loss_i2t = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels) # each image → its caption loss_t2i = F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels) # each caption → its image return (loss_i2t + loss_t2i) / 2 ``` **The crucial consequence:** after training, an image of a blue pottery vase and the text "a blue pottery vase" land near each other in the same 512-dimensional space. You can compute cosine similarity between a *picture* and a *sentence* — which is exactly the operation from Day 6, now working across modalities. ##### Zero-shot classification with CLIP ```python import torch from PIL import Image from transformers import CLIPProcessor, CLIPModel model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32") processor = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32") model.eval() image = Image.open("product_8821.jpg") # Prompt templates matter — CLIP was trained on caption-like text categories = ["block printed cotton fabric", "blue pottery vase", "lac bangles", "mojari juti footwear", "miniature painting", "brass utensil"] texts = [f"a photo of {c}" for c in categories] inputs = processor(text=texts, images=image, return_tensors="pt", padding=True) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model(**inputs) probs = outputs.logits_per_image.softmax(dim=1)[0] for cat, p in sorted(zip(categories, probs.tolist()), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:3]: print(f"{p:.3f} {cat}") ``` **Two practical details.** The `"a photo of {}"` template is not decoration — CLIP was trained on captions, so phrasing your labels as captions typically gains several points over bare class names. And ensembling multiple templates (`"a photo of a {}"`, `"a close-up photo of a {}"`, `"a product photo of a {}"`) and averaging the text embeddings gains a little more. **Cross-modal search** falls out of the same space: ```python import numpy as np def embed_images(paths, batch_size=32): vecs = [] for i in range(0, len(paths), batch_size): imgs = [Image.open(p).convert("RGB") for p in paths[i:i+batch_size]] inp = processor(images=imgs, return_tensors="pt", padding=True) with torch.no_grad(): v = model.get_image_features(**inp) vecs.append(torch.nn.functional.normalize(v, dim=-1).numpy()) return np.vstack(vecs) def search_images(query, image_embeds, paths, k=5): inp = processor(text=[query], return_tensors="pt", padding=True) with torch.no_grad(): q = model.get_text_features(**inp) q = torch.nn.functional.normalize(q, dim=-1).numpy()[0] scores = image_embeds @ q top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k] return [(paths[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top] catalogue = embed_images(all_product_paths) for path, score in search_images("indigo blue handblock print with floral motif", catalogue, all_product_paths): print(f"{score:.3f} {path}") ``` Those embeddings go straight into the vector database from Day 34. **CLIP image vectors and CLIP text vectors are interchangeable in the same index** — which means one Chroma collection can serve text-to-image, image-to-image, and image-to-text search. CLIP's limitations are worth knowing: it is weak on counting, spatial relations ("the cup left of the book"), fine-grained distinctions, and rendered text. Its successor SigLIP uses a pairwise sigmoid loss instead of softmax and generally performs better. ##### Vision-language models CLIP compares images and text. A **vision-language model** generates text *about* an image — captioning, visual question answering, document understanding, OCR-plus-reasoning. The standard architecture is more modular than people expect: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Image"] --> B["Vision encoder
(often CLIP ViT)"] B --> C["Projection layer
vision dims → LLM dims"] C --> D["Image tokens
e.g. 576 tokens"] E["Text prompt"] --> F["Tokenizer"] F --> G["Text tokens"] D --> H["LLM
(Llama, Vicuna, ...)"] G --> H H --> I["Generated text"] ``` **LLaVA's insight** was that you can take a frozen CLIP vision encoder, a frozen LLM, and train only a small projection layer between them — turning image patches into things the LLM treats as tokens. The whole model becomes multimodal for a fraction of the cost of training from scratch. ```python import torch from PIL import Image from transformers import AutoProcessor, LlavaForConditionalGeneration model_id = "llava-hf/llava-1.5-7b-hf" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = LlavaForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained( model_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto" ) image = Image.open("damaged_parcel.jpg") prompt = ("USER: \nThis is a customer's photo of a delivered parcel. " "Describe any visible damage and whether the seal is intact. " "Answer in two sentences.\nASSISTANT:") inputs = processor(text=prompt, images=image, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda", torch.float16) with torch.no_grad(): out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=150, do_sample=False) print(processor.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True).split("ASSISTANT:")[-1].strip()) ``` Using a hosted VLM through an API is often simpler: ```python import base64 from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() with open("invoice.jpg", "rb") as f: b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "Extract from this Indian GST invoice as JSON: vendor_name, gstin, " "invoice_number, invoice_date (YYYY-MM-DD), total_amount. " "Use null for anything not visible. Return only JSON."}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{b64}", "detail": "high"}}, ], }], temperature=0.0, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` **A cost note that surprises people:** images consume tokens. A high-detail 1024×1024 image is roughly 750–1,100 tokens depending on the provider. Use `detail: "low"` (about 85 tokens) when you only need the gist, and resize images before sending — uploading a 4000×3000 phone photo when 1024px suffices wastes real money at volume. Practical VLM applications: invoice and receipt extraction, damage assessment for insurance and logistics claims, accessibility alt-text generation, chart and diagram interpretation, and screenshot-based UI debugging. ##### Whisper and speech Whisper (OpenAI, 2022) is an encoder-decoder transformer trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio. It transcribes, translates, and detects language — and it handles accented English and Indian languages notably better than most predecessors. ```python import whisper model = whisper.load_model("small") # tiny/base/small/medium/large-v3 result = model.transcribe( "customer_call.mp3", language="hi", # or None to auto-detect task="transcribe", # or "translate" → always outputs English fp16=True, verbose=False, ) print(result["text"]) for seg in result["segments"][:3]: print(f"[{seg['start']:.1f}s - {seg['end']:.1f}s] {seg['text']}") ``` | Model | Params | VRAM | Speed | Use | |---|---|---|---|---| | tiny | 39M | ~1 GB | 32× | Quick drafts | | base | 74M | ~1 GB | 16× | Real-time on CPU | | **small** | 244M | ~2 GB | 6× | **Good default** | | medium | 769M | ~5 GB | 2× | High accuracy | | large-v3 | 1550M | ~10 GB | 1× | Best, multilingual | For Indian languages specifically, `large-v3` is substantially better than the smaller variants, and AI4Bharat's **IndicWhisper** is fine-tuned for Indian languages and accents — worth evaluating if that is your use case. `faster-whisper` (CTranslate2) gives roughly 4× speedup at equal accuracy. Whisper's `task="translate"` only translates *into* English, which trips people up. For other target languages, transcribe first, then translate with an LLM. ##### Composing modalities The interesting systems chain these together: ```python def voice_product_query(audio_path, catalogue_embeds, paths, vlm_client): """Voice → text → image search → grounded answer.""" # 1. Speech to text transcript = whisper_model.transcribe(audio_path)["text"] # 2. Text to image search via CLIP hits = search_images(transcript, catalogue_embeds, paths, k=3) # 3. VLM describes the top match, grounded in the actual image description = describe_image(hits[0][0], f"A customer asked: '{transcript}'. " f"Describe this product and why it matches.") return {"query": transcript, "matches": [{"path": p, "score": s} for p, s in hits], "answer": description} ``` Three models, three modalities, one pipeline. For a marketplace serving users who prefer speaking Hindi or Tamil over typing, this removes a genuine accessibility barrier. ##### Common mistakes - **Bare class names in CLIP** instead of caption-style prompts like `"a photo of {}"`. - **Forgetting to normalise** embeddings before cosine similarity. - **Mixing embeddings from different CLIP variants** — they are not comparable. - **Expecting CLIP to count or handle spatial relations.** It cannot. - **Sending full-resolution photos to a VLM API**, paying for tokens you do not need. - **`detail: "high"` for every image** when `"low"` would do. - **Trusting VLM output on dense documents without verification** — OCR errors on handwriting and low-quality scans are common. - **Whisper `tiny` for Indian languages**, where the accuracy gap to `large-v3` is large. - **Assuming `task="translate"` goes to your target language.** It only outputs English. - **No audio preprocessing** — Whisper expects 16 kHz mono; noisy input degrades it badly. - **Ignoring that images carry EXIF and can contain PII**, relevant under the DPDP Act. ##### Hands-on: match, then question Your practical task uses CLIP to match images to captions and a VLM to answer questions about an image. For the CLIP half, build a small set of 20 images and 20 captions, compute the full similarity matrix, and check how often the diagonal wins — that is CLIP's contrastive objective, evaluated. For the VLM half, ask a question requiring actual visual reasoning ("how many items are on the table?") and note where it fails; those failures map exactly onto the limitations listed above. The mini project is a multimodal assistant taking an image plus a question, with Whisper voice input. Gradio handles both file upload and microphone input natively, which makes this quicker than it sounds. Test with Hindi or Tamil voice input if you can — Whisper's multilingual handling is genuinely impressive, and demonstrating it makes the project stand out. Keep the grounding discipline from Day 35: the answer should describe what is *in* the image, and the model should say so when it cannot tell. The assignment explains CLIP's contrastive training with a diagram. Draw the N×N similarity matrix explicitly, mark the diagonal as positives and everything else as negatives, and show the symmetric loss over rows and columns. Then explain the payoff — that a single shared space enables zero-shot classification, text-to-image search, and image-to-image search with no task-specific training. That last point is what makes CLIP worth a day of study. ##### Key takeaways - **Contrastive training puts images and text in one embedding space**, making a picture and a sentence directly comparable by cosine similarity. - **CLIP gives you zero-shot classification and cross-modal search with no labelled data** — phrase labels as captions, and the embeddings drop straight into your vector database. - **Vision-language models bolt a vision encoder onto an LLM through a small projection layer**, which is why LLaVA-style models are cheap to build and good at document extraction. - **Whisper handles multilingual and accented speech well**, but size matters for Indian languages and `task="translate"` only ever outputs English. - **Images cost tokens.** Resize before sending, use low detail when you only need the gist, and know that counting and spatial reasoning remain genuine weaknesses across all these models.
